title: In praise of commercial culture
gist: A wide-ranging Yglesias mailbag whose through-line is that commercial and competitive pressure disciplines institutions: art forms that lose mass-market accountability (literary fiction, live theater) turn insular, while movies stay vital because artistic and profit aspirations coexist. Along the way he declares real concern that AI kills everyone via U.S.-China deployment races, argues gerrymandering's worst damage is nationalizing state politics, says AIPAC's 15-year Iran litmus test plus a cost-of-living-raising war torched the 'pro-Israel' brand among Democrats, and insists party realignment runs through the 2028 presidential primary rather than downballot races.

themes.theme: AI risk and the US-China race

insights.claim: The U.S.-China geopolitical rivalry creates bad incentives for both countries to deploy AI systems excessively aggressively and recklessly, without understanding the real workings and capabilities of what they are shipping.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Geopolitical competition, not commercial competition, is the load-bearing driver of AI deployment risk — and of the political appetite to regulate it.
insights.quote: the U.S.-China geopolitical rivalry creates bad incentives for both countries to facilitate excessively aggressive and excessively reckless deployment
insights.locator: Someone told me the other day

insights.claim: Both prevailing positions on AI are wrong: the left view that everything about A.I. is terrible except the existential risk, which it dismisses as bubble hype, and the libertarian techno-optimist fallacy of inferring that every technological advance is good from the fact that progress has been good on average.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Signals that AI-safety concern is migrating into mainstream center-left commentary rather than staying a fringe or industry-aligned position.
insights.quote: a libertarian techno-optimist's fallacy of inferring
insights.locator: There is a view on the left

insights.claim: AI safety is now an explicit criterion in Democratic candidate endorsements, with Alex Bores, Manny Rutinel and Scott Wiener all being backed at least partly on that basis.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that AI regulation is becoming a Democratic primary litmus issue — a medium-term regulatory risk for AI developers.
insights.locator: It's why Alex Bores was on the November donation recommendations list

insights.claim: Republicans hold a trifecta in New Hampshire and are deliberately not redrawing the state's House maps, a restraint that reduces the pressure on state moderates to vote them out.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A live counterexample to the redistricting arms race, and a marker of where GOP moderation still has electoral value.
insights.quote: Republicans have a trifecta in New Hampshire and are not using it to redraw the state's House maps
insights.locator: I think it's pretty easy to imagine a scenario

insights.claim: Blue states including Virginia, Maryland, New York and Colorado should engage in retaliatory gerrymandering before 2028 because asymmetrical intra-census redistricting has left the median House seat way to the right of the national average.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Blue-state map fights over the next two years are a direct determinant of 2028 House control odds.
insights.quote: Right now the median House seat is way to the right of the national average
insights.locator: But looking ahead to the 2028 cycle

insights.claim: Gerrymandering's worst effect is downstream nationalization: it makes out-of-state actors invested in state races purely for House-map consequences, so a national ban would improve state politics more than it improves Congress.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A non-obvious second-order argument — reform advocates and donors misallocate attention by focusing on the congressional effect.
insights.quote: It is very bad for the state of Wisconsin to have lots of people who don't live in Wisconsin be invested in the outcome of its state races
insights.locator: That being said, the real moral of this story

insights.claim: A YIMBY-oriented Republican governor can be preferable to a left-wing Democrat in an already-progressive blue state — the Phil Scott model in Vermont — but Trump-orchestrated gerrymandering, January 6 and election denial now import federal concerns into state races.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains why split-ticket moderation is collapsing: federalized stakes are crowding out state-level policy evaluation.
insights.quote: That's basically how Phil Scott keeps winning in Vermont.
insights.locator: BBDC: What is the most realistic scenario

insights.claim: The Biden administration ran sanctions policy and domestic drilling policy in separate silos, each as its own tradeoff against cheap oil, when an integrated approach — cracking down on Russian and Iranian production while expanding domestic supply — would have been better for the environment, the economy and foreign policy simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A template for spotting win-win-win policy trades that siloed institutions systematically miss — and for anticipating how a future administration could reprice oil supply.
insights.quote: you could have gotten an outcome that was better for the environment, better for the American economy, and better for American foreign-policy objectives
insights.locator: For those who missed the post

insights.claim: Because farm animals are so numerous, very small and low-cost improvements in how they are treated deliver far more suffering-alleviation per dollar than blocking development over habitat loss.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Cost-effectiveness reasoning that could redirect environmental-advocacy resources — and shift where development-blocking litigation risk actually lands.
insights.quote: very incremental low-cost improvements in their well-being have huge benefits
insights.locator: But to the extent that animal welfare is the hook

themes.theme: The Iran war rewires Democratic politics

insights.claim: AIPAC spent 15 years setting the pro-Israel bar at orienting American regional foreign policy around Israel's view of Iran, a standard very few Democrats could meet — and when the resulting war arrived it torched the brand image of being 'pro-Israel.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The intra-Democratic shift on Israel is a durable brand collapse driven by the war's cost, not a transient reaction — expect it to persist into 2028 primaries.
insights.quote: the war has just totally torched the brand image of “pro-Israel”
insights.locator: Nik Gupta: I remember you called the Iran war

insights.claim: The Iran war became instantly super-unpopular because of its negative impact on Americans' economic well-being, meaning voters are judging foreign policy through a cost-of-living lens.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Foreign-policy escalation now transmits directly to domestic political risk via energy and consumer prices — a key linkage for macro-political forecasting.
insights.quote: it instantly became super-unpopular due to the negative impact on Americans' economic well-being
insights.locator: That's a ridiculous thing to ask of people

insights.claim: The backlash against a discredited pro-Israel establishment does not logically require flipping to totalizing investment in Palestinian nationalism, but most voters' engagement is fuzzy enough that the flip happens anyway.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Predicts overshoot in Democratic primary positioning — the moderate middle ground is unlikely to be occupied.
insights.locator: The fact that this is all bad and terrible

insights.claim: Art forms decay into insularity when they lose their commercial mass-market framing: 19th-century literary fiction was mainstream business, whereas today literary fiction is a small niche not expected to generate big sales and sustained by workshops, connections and an incestuous circle of favor-granting.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A general model of institutional decline applicable well beyond the arts — when output stops being tested by paying customers, quality signals degrade into in-group status.
insights.quote: a somewhat incestuous circle of favor-granting
insights.locator: This is definitely part of it

insights.claim: Commercial constraints shaped canonical literature directly, since the major works of Charles Dickens and Fyodor Dostoevsky were published serially and their choices about pace and structure were really commercial dictates.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Undercuts the assumption that market pressure and artistic merit trade off — the historical record shows they co-produced the canon.
insights.quote: some of the literary choices being made about pace and structure were really commercial dictates
insights.locator: The major works of Charles Dickens

insights.claim: American live theater's problem is that original plays carry no expectation of mainstream success, so producers aren't really trying to reach general audiences and instead serve an insular world of theater enthusiasts.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Diagnoses theater's demand problem as a supply-side incentive failure, which implies subsidies alone won't reverse it.
insights.quote: there's no expectation that an original play is going to be a hit success with mainstream audiences. As a result, they're not really trying.
insights.locator: But I was talking about living right near the Studio Theatre

insights.claim: The opening-act test distinguishes healthy from unhealthy art markets: at a rock club the opener is presented in the good-faith belief the audience will enjoy it, while a symphony's contemporary curtain-raiser is something 90 percent of attendees don't care about.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A cheap diagnostic for whether an institution is actually serving its audience or performing obligation to an in-group.
insights.quote: there is a good-faith belief that the audience will genuinely enjoy the opener
insights.locator: If you go to a rock show at the 9:30 Club

insights.claim: Movies remain vital because artistic and commercial aspirations coexist in the same product, and a director's track record of delivering studio profits earns running room to pursue personal ideas without begging for grant money or appealing to a narrow in-group.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The commercial-track-record mechanism is what funds artistic risk — relevant to how studios and platforms should structure creative bets.
insights.quote: the ability to achieve commercial success is also freeing
insights.locator: To me, part of what's interesting and vital about movies

insights.claim: Intellectual property law is a pure legislative and judicial contrivance meant to advance the general interest, and the current regime in which a digital purchase isn't really a purchase fails that test.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A live regulatory risk for digital storefronts and licensing-dependent platforms if durable-ownership rules ever get legislated.
insights.quote: all aspects of intellectual property law are pure legislative and judicial contrivances
insights.locator: Mathew: With playstation customers losing digital movies

insights.claim: It is absurd but currently true that owning a film with certainty requires buying physical media, and there should be a legal status granting digital purchases the irrevocable rights associated with ownership.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: If enacted, this would force platforms to carry perpetual licensing liabilities — a real cost line for streaming and console storefronts.
insights.quote: if you really want to own a film and be sure you'll have access to it, you have to buy it on physical media

themes.theme: How factions actually take over parties

insights.claim: Parties are redefined through presidential primaries rather than dozens of downballot races — Trump won one primary and remade the GOP on immigration and Social Security, while Bernie Sanders lost in 2016 but built a durable factional enterprise on a clear message.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Tells you where to watch for genuine party realignment: the 2028 presidential primary, not the 2026 downballot cycle.
insights.quote: Trump won a presidential primary and redefined the party.

insights.claim: Blue Dog overperformers like Marie Glusenkamp Perez cannot win presidential primaries because the primary electorate demands feisty aggressive partisanship, which is exactly what a member representing a Trump district cannot safely deliver.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Structural reason the moderate-savior scenario keeps failing — worth discounting any 'Blue Dog for president' narrative.
insights.quote: one thing the primary electorate definitely demands is feisty and aggressive partisanship

insights.claim: First-term senators such as Elissa Slotkin and Ruben Gallego have the structural advantage of performing feisty partisanship through 2028 and then shifting into dealmaking mode in time for 2030 re-election.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Names the two most structurally advantaged 2028 Democratic contenders on positioning grounds rather than polling.
insights.quote: they can do feisty partisanship through 2028 and then if necessary shift into dealmaking mode in time for 2030

insights.claim: The first Democratic politicians to break from the advocacy groups pay a reputational penalty that only disappears if the party moves en masse, which is why change requires a single high-impact primary campaign rather than incremental defection.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A coordination-problem framing that predicts stasis until 2028 — useful for timing any thesis about Democratic policy moderation.
